I grew up in a religious household, but it wasn't strictly so. I was allowed to find my own beliefs, with the most stern warnings being that I would be judged when I died and that there was only one path to God.

When I grew up, years later, I had spent the majority of my adolescence as a rather militant atheist. I blamed religion for all the world's ills, and rejected wholly what I considered a corny philosophy akin to a poster of a cat that says "hang in there". I saw nothing that I could say I took as evidence of a God's existence, and reveled in my philosophical understandings of his non-existence. I felt self - righteous in the knowledge that the dumb, ignorant masses had to hold on to an archaic belief that I thought had brought untold misery to the world.

Fast forward to my late twenties. I had been involved with drugs for a large portion of my life. I went to rehab and met quite a few junkies, and started using intravenous heroin when the worst I had done before my arrest was to occasionally smoke cannabis and pop a couple Xanax bars.

I was lost. I was alone. I was living with my family, physically, but not spiritually. I constantly fought them, and threw their accusations of worry to the floor. I really believe that I wanted to die, and I did in fact, several times do exactly that. I caused permanent damage to my neck and shoulder when I overdosed and passed out, compressing an artery for several hours. It still haunts me every second of my life.

When I turned thirty, I found a girl who I found beautiful, dark, mysterious. She was everything I had ever lusted after. Everything I had ever dreamed of. She fit every archetype of my perfect mate. She was smart, intellectual, beautiful, and absolutely insane.

My girlfriends' parents are both doctors, so I took their observations as truth. My girlfriend suffers from schizoaffective disorder. She suffered an emotional and psychological breakdown, and came to believe that she was immortal. She still struggles with this delusion on a daily basis. But I love her, and I romanticized her mental illness as ultimate eccentricity. Quirkiness. Beautiful insanity, such as Van Gough or Einstein.

I don't remember when I came to believe again in God. I think it was the state of the world, and my gradual immersion back into society and the workforce. I began to see things that I couldn't explain. Things that were beyond the trivial gnosis of the templi orientalis. Things that I could not rectify with my feeble understanding of the world.

Today. Now. I'm working full time. I make ends meet as well as I can. I have faith now that no one can take from me, and it is miraculous. I feel something in me that I haven't felt in twenty years. I support my love, my mystery, my girlfriend, as well as I can. She is innocent, and misguided. I feel great strain in our relationship in that she is still convinced that becoming one with God is an absolution of loss of individuality, which she worships above all else.
